topics.name: Communication process and principles
topics.why: Lots of named lists (principles, 7 Cs, the 9 sending rules). Flashcards first, then test yourself.
topics.notes:
The communication cycle: Sender → encoding (turning the idea into words, symbols, gestures) → message → channel (medium) → receiver → decoding (interpreting the meaning) → feedback back to the sender. Noise can disrupt any stage.

Principles of communication (Week 2):

  • Communication is (often) intentional, purposeful and consciously motivated. Reactive communication makes small issues become big problems, and you spend more time fixing than building.
  • Intentional communication: conveying messages with clarity, empathy and purpose, mindful of not just what is said but how, when and why. Effective communication builds teams, drives change and shapes culture. Towers Watson found companies with highly effective communication enjoy 47% higher total returns to shareholders.
  • Communication is inevitable: you communicate even when you don't mean to (clothing, haircut, an expressionless face staring out the window).
  • Communication is irreversible: you can turn grapes into wine but not wine into grapes. Once you press send, it's impossible to take back.
  • Communication is unrepeatable: no exchange can be exactly recreated.
  • Communication requires ethical choices: freedom of speech doesn't mean you can say anything you please. Words can nurture or destroy, and can be weaponised. Plagiarism and harassment are examples.
  • Communication has limitations: it can't solve all interpersonal problems. Other skills are needed (flexibility, forgiveness, openness to change).

Case used in class: Macklemore removed from Ed Sheeran's tour. The team stayed silent too long, and silence was "decoded" by the audience as outrage.

Sending messages effectively (9): be direct · own your message · be complete and specific · state your needs clearly · separate fact from opinion · focus on one thing at a time · deliver messages immediately · avoid hidden agendas · be supportive and consistent.

The 7 Cs: Completeness, Correctness, Conciseness, Courtesy, Clarity, Consideration, Concreteness (and coherence).

How to practise intentional communication (12 steps): 1 know your purpose (inform, persuade, entertain) · 2 understand your audience · 3 plan your message · 4 choose your words carefully (avoid jargon) · 5 be concise · 6 listen actively · 7 use the right tone · 8 ask for feedback (timely, accurate, actionable) · 9 be aware of non-verbal cues · 10 practise empathy · 11 be patient · 12 reflect and improve (Gibbs Reflective Cycle, 1988).

Dialogic communication: speaker and listener create meaning together. It's not a monologue, the speaker doesn't force beliefs on the audience, and both take an active role.

topics.name: Communication barriers
topics.why: Know each barrier type and an example. Questions will give a scenario and ask which barrier it is.
topics.notes:
Barriers come from the sender, the receiver and technology/transmission.

TypeWhat it is
Internal noiseInside sender and receiver: beliefs and values, faulty assumptions, trigger or 'hot button' words, defensiveness
External noiseOutside them: easier to control than internal noise; includes technology
Semantic noiseThe receiver doesn't understand a word or gesture: different cultures, technicians using jargon with laypeople
GapsDifferences between people: gender, age, ethnicity, race, status, sexual orientation, generation
Sender barriersHow much they know about the subject, indecision about how to present it, the order of presentation, unfamiliar audience, emotional conflict, lack of experience
Receiver barriersSurroundings, physical condition, failure to pay attention (several messages at once, boredom), not understanding words, personal interests, emotional responses
Transmission barriersIllegible material, poor acoustics, too many transmission links, conflicting messages
Selective perceptionHearing or seeing only what fits what you already believe or expect

Barriers to listening (4 categories): internal distractions, external distractions, personal biases, conflicting demands.

Factors that reduce listening skills: the fast pace of everyday life, media training us to be passive listeners, commercials and "mini-messages", our own thoughts and feelings (daydreaming, anxiety, illness, fatigue), "scriptwriting" (planning what to say next), defensive listeners who prejudge, and cultural differences.

topics.name: Active listening
topics.why: SOLER, the 4 steps, hearing vs listening and the pyramid: definition questions.
topics.notes:
Hearing is not listening. "Hearing is with the ears, listening is with the mind."

HearingListening
Accidental, involuntary, effortlessFocused, voluntary, intentional
A physical, passive processA mental and physical, active process. It needs concentration and leads to learning

The average person understands only 30% of what they hear. Employees and managers spend 42–63% of their workday listening (Wolvin and Coakley, 1991), and listening is the most critical communication skill affecting organisational behaviour.

Listening: 4 steps: 1 Hear · 2 Interpret (decode) · 3 Understand (link to other concepts) · 4 Recall (remember).

Stages of active listening (pyramid, bottom up): S.O.L.E.R. body language → paraphrasing and asking questions → meaning and reflection → empathy → action.

SOLER = Sit squarely · Open posture · Lean slightly in · Eye contact (without staring) · Relax

Active listening tips: Listen (don't multitask or fake-listen) · Feedback (compassionate, constructive) · Confirm (repeat and paraphrase: "if I heard you correctly…") · Ask (a relevant follow-up question).

Activity list: read non-verbals, avoid distraction, apply the ideas, paraphrase, know your effect on the sender.

Competent listeners have more successful relationships, more professional success, solve problems better, are more engaged citizens, and learn from other speakers. Listening also matters in consumer behaviour (it shapes perceptions and purchase decisions) and in negotiation.

Critical thinking in listening means evaluating claims on well-supported reasons, evaluating evidence for accuracy and credibility, and watching for assumptions and biases. "Most people do not listen with the intent to understand; they listen with the intent to reply."

topics.name: Emotional intelligence
topics.why: Goleman's 5 elements, the types of empathy and intrinsic vs extrinsic motivation.
topics.notes:
Goleman's 5 elements of emotional intelligence (EQ): self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, social skills.

Low EIHigh EI
'You always make me feel…''I feel…'
Can't share feelings verbally; negative feelings dominateOpen expression of emotions; not preoccupied with negatives
Not perceptive to others' feelings; carries grudgesIdentifies others' feelings; emotionally resilient
Acts without reasoning; poor listenerDecisions based on feelings and logic; good listener
'Hits out' when there's a problemTalks about problems

Higher EI in education: manages transitions better, less likely to drop out, higher qualifications, better career prospects.

Self-awareness: looking inward, thinking deeply about your behaviour, knowing your actions match your values. Personality tools: Big Five (OCEAN), Myers-Briggs (use with caution). Introverts are roughly 25–40% of people and recharge alone. Extroverts are 60–75% and are energised by others.

Self-regulation: managing your emotions and impulses. Zimmerman (2002) self-regulated learning: planning → monitoring → reflection.

Motivation (Latin movere, to move). Intrinsic: the activity is the reward. Extrinsic: to earn a reward or avoid punishment. Skinner's reinforcement theory and the law of effect: behaviour with positive consequences tends to be repeated. Maslow's hierarchy: only about 1 in 100 people become fully self-actualised.

Empathy is sensing others' emotions and imagining what they think or feel. Three types: affective (feeling what they feel), somatic (a physical reaction) and cognitive (understanding their thoughts). The empathy trap is being overwhelmed and neglecting your own needs.

topics.name: Group theory and team dynamics
topics.why: The biggest slide deck: Tuckman, groupthink (Challenger) and social loafing (Ringelmann).
topics.notes:
A team is two or more people who interact to accomplish goals or meet needs. All teams are groups, but not all groups are teams: teams work more intensely together towards a specific, over-riding goal.

Teams contribute through synergy (performance enhancers), responsiveness to customers (cross-functional teams), innovation and as motivators. A formal group is set up by managers for organisational goals. An informal group is formed by employees for their own goals or needs. Team types: committee, problem-solving, project, creative, cross-functional.

Large groups: more resources, division of labour, more learning and diversity · but communication and coordination problems, lower motivation, trust and accountability.

Effective teams: synergy, shared purpose, clear and challenging goals, a diverse mix, the right size, psychological safety, team before individual, open and honest communication.

Task interdependence: pooled (separate contributions added together) · sequential (tasks in a set order, like writer then editor: clear but risks bottlenecks) · reciprocal (each depends fully on the others, like designer and developer: innovative but complex).

Tuckman's stages: Forming (getting to know each other; can be slowest) → Storming (conflict; has to happen to set rules) → Norming (close ties and consensus; dangerous, as biases solidify) → Performing (real work; sometimes never reached) → Adjourning (temporary groups disband).

Norms are shared rules most members follow. Members conform to get rewards, imitate respected members, or because it feels right. A deviant is pressured to conform, expelled, or the norms change. Cohesiveness is measured by participation, conformity and emphasis on group goals. A balance of conformity and deviance is healthy.

Groupthink is "a process of flawed decision making that occurs as a result of strong pressures among group members to reach an agreement" (Gruman, Schneider and Coutts, 2017). Challenger, 28 Jan 1986: the O-rings only worked above 53°F, and it was 36°F at launch. National, political and media pressure (Reagan's State of the Union that night) pushed the launch through. To counteract it: assign a critical evaluator, have trusted outsiders scrutinise decisions, hold meetings for raising misgivings, split into subgroups, and listen to dissenting views.

Social loafing is putting in less effort in a group than alone. Ringelmann (1913) rope-pulling: people pulled less in groups, and the 1974 replication showed it's motivational, not coordination. Causes: low motivation, diffusion of responsibility (like the bystander effect), group size, and expectations that others will slack. Fix it by making individual contributions identifiable, keeping groups small, valuing every contribution, and rewarding both individual and group performance.

Social facilitation: the presence of others (real, implied or imagined) improves performance. Co-action effect: others doing the same task. Audience effect: performing in front of others. Influenced by physiological, cognitive and affective factors.

Belbin's team roles (linked on Moodle): Plant, Resource Investigator, Co-ordinator, Shaper, Monitor Evaluator, Teamworker, Implementer, Completer Finisher, Specialist.

topics.name: Academic writing and presentation skills
topics.why: The Academic Writing lectures are this week. Add your own notes from them.
topics.notes:
The Academic Writing lectures are on 17 and 20 Nov and their slides aren't on Moodle yet. These are standard points. Add your own notes from the lectures.

  • Harvard referencing: in-text (Author, Year) or Author (Year), e.g. (Wolvin and Coakley, 1991). A full reference list at the end, alphabetical by author.
  • Academic tone: formal, objective, third person, no contractions or slang.
  • Structure: introduction (what you'll argue) → body paragraphs (one point each, with evidence) → conclusion (no new information).
  • Paraphrase in your own words and still cite it. Direct quotes go in quotation marks with a page number.
  • Use credible sources: TUS Library and Google Scholar (from the Week 2 slides).
  • Plagiarism is an ethical issue: communication requires ethical choices.

Presentation skills (also fair game): THINK and plan (aim: inform, persuade or request · audience · context · likely reaction). Voice: project from the diaphragm, a strong voice not a loud one, vary pace, pitch, inflection, emphasis and pause, and avoid inaudibility (clenched teeth). Over 50% of communication is non-verbal, and congruence means your body language must match your words. On the day: be early, don't sway or chew gum, keep your hands visible, and clarify a question before answering.

info.presentation:
Group presentation (20%). Analyse one effective communicator (ideally someone niche) using module theory: communication principles, active listening, non-verbal communication, EI.

  • Tue 17 Nov lecture: tell Kelly which date and time slot your group wants. Each lab hour only fits 3–4 groups.
  • Slots left on Moodle: Tue 17 Nov 4–6pm (1A12) · Wed 18 Nov 11am–1pm (8A107) and 4–6pm (1A12) · Thu 19 Nov 11am–1pm (1A17) and 2–4pm (1A13) · Tue 24 Nov 4–6pm (1A12) · Wed 25 Nov 11am–1pm (8A107) and 4–6pm (1A12) · Thu 26 Nov 11am–1pm (1A17). Thu 26 Nov 2–3pm is fully booked.
  • Submission (changed 13 Nov): the group leader shares the PowerPoint with kelly.browne@tus.ie via OneDrive before 9am on the morning of your presentation, with editing rights.
  • File name: every member's name, e.g. Tomdunne_Marysheehy_Karenfoley_BusComsAssessment2.pptx. Incorrectly named files are rejected. Names also go on the opening slide.
  • Maximum 8 slides, including title, activity, conclusion and reference slides. Use Harvard referencing.
  • Include an audience activity and a 2-minute Q&A answered as a group.
  • Everyone must be present and deliver part of it to get the team mark. Check the rubric on Moodle for how delivery is marked.
